latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Host inability to eliminate EBV-infected lymphocytes despite persistent antigen exposure; the upstream permissive substrate for chronic active EBV disease rather than ordinary self-limited infectious mononucleosis.
Persistent oligoclonal or monoclonal expansion of EBV-infected cytotoxic T cells or NK cells; the dominant biology in most systemic CAEBV and the driver of inflammatory organ infiltration.
Persistent EBV-positive B-cell expansion seen in a minority of CAEBV phenotypes and in some Western cohorts; important because CD20-targeted therapy can reduce this compartment.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Intermittent EBV lytic reactivation and DNAemia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Variable lytic EBV replication and release of EBV DNA on top of the infected lymphocyte reservoir; explains fluctuating peripheral blood viral load and limited antiviral responsiveness.
IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-10, TNF, and related inflammatory signaling from EBV-infected lymphocytes and reactive macrophages; produces recurrent fever, fatigue, wasting, CRP, ferritin, and LDH elevation.

EBV-positive lymphoid infiltration and reactive expansion in lymph nodes, spleen, liver, marrow, and related mononuclear phagocyte compartments; produces lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, LDH elevation, and sequestration cytopenias.

Sinusoidal, portal, or parenchymal infiltration by EBV-positive lymphocytes with immune hepatocyte injury; causes recurrent transaminitis, cholestasis, jaundice, hypoalbuminemia, and occasionally hepatic failure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cytopenia from marrow involvement, hypersplenism, and inflammation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Combined marrow infiltration, cytokine marrow suppression, hemophagocytic pressure, and splenic sequestration; produces leukopenia, neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cutaneous and mucosal EBV-positive lymphoid infiltration
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Skin and mucosal infiltration by EBV-positive cytotoxic lymphocytes; includes hydroa vacciniforme-like lesions, severe mosquito bite allergy, papules/nodules, oral ulcers, and panniculitis-like subcutaneous lesions.

EBV-positive lymphoid infiltration or vasculitic injury in gastrointestinal tract, lung, kidney, eye/orbit, central nervous system, serosal surfaces, and blood vessels; drives the heterogeneous organ-disease spectrum.

Escalation from chronic EBV lymphoproliferation into macrophage activation and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis; causes severe fever, ferritin/sCD25 elevation, hypofibrinogenemia, cytopenias, bleeding, and multiorgan failure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Transformation to EBV-positive T/NK or B-cell lymphoma
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Accumulation of malignant features in the EBV-infected clone, including NK/T-cell lymphoma, aggressive NK-cell leukemia, systemic T-cell lymphoma, or B-cell lymphoproliferative disease; a late high-mortality CAEBV event.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Insufficient EBV-specific cytotoxic clearance permits persistence and expansion of EBV-infected T/NK cells.
Some CAEBV phenotypes retain EBV primarily in B cells when host B-cell EBV control fails.
The infected lymphocyte reservoir is the substrate for intermittent EBV DNAemia.
EBV-infected cytotoxic lymphocytes and reactive macrophages produce the chronic inflammatory phenotype.
The infected clone infiltrates lymphoid and reticuloendothelial tissues.
CAEBV commonly shows T/NK-cell skin and mucosal infiltration in hydroa vacciniforme-like, mosquito-bite, ulcerative, or nodular patterns.
Systemic CAEBV can infiltrate gastrointestinal, pulmonary, renal, ocular, CNS, serosal, and vascular tissues.
Liver is a frequent CAEBV target organ, with sinusoidal and portal lymphocytic infiltration.
Marrow involvement, splenic sequestration, and inflammatory marrow suppression create cytopenias.
T/NK CAEBV is a recognized substrate for EBV-associated HLH.
The infected T/NK clone can evolve into NK/T-cell lymphoma, systemic T-cell lymphoma, or aggressive NK-cell leukemia.
EBV-positive B-cell proliferation can also produce fever, lymphadenopathy, and inflammatory organ injury.
Peripheral blood EBV DNA tracks EBV-infected cells and intermittent lytic reactivation.
Cell-sorted EBER, flow-FISH, or tissue IHC can identify the infected T/NK lineage.
B-cell CAEBV and EBV-positive B-cell lymphoproliferation are identified by tissue or sorted-cell studies.
Affected tissue shows EBV-encoded RNA-positive lymphoid infiltrates.
Persistent or intermittent fever is the most common clinical manifestation of CAEBV.
CAEBV usually appears as recurrent or prolonged mononucleosis-like fever rather than a short acute viral syndrome.
Current fever often persists for weeks during flare periods.
CAEBV is defined by chronic or recurrent illness over months to years.
Systemic inflammation causes fatigue and malaise.
IL-6 axis activity can raise CRP, often less specifically than bacterial sepsis.
Tissue infiltration, lymphocyte turnover, liver injury, and HLH can raise LDH.
Lymphadenopathy is common in CAEBV and may be cervical, generalized, or deep nodal.
Nodal burden increases with lymphoid infiltration.
Splenic infiltration and reticuloendothelial activation produce splenomegaly.
Hepatic infiltration and inflammation often produce hepatomegaly.
CAEBV hepatitis can markedly elevate AST.
CAEBV hepatitis can markedly elevate ALT.
Cholestasis and hepatic dysfunction can produce jaundice and total bilirubin elevation.
Conjugated bilirubin rises with CAEBV cholestatic hepatitis.
Cholestatic injury can raise alkaline phosphatase.
Chronic inflammation, hepatic dysfunction, and enteric loss can lower albumin.
Leukopenia can occur from marrow suppression or infiltration; some cases instead show lymphocyte expansion.
Neutropenia can arise from marrow involvement, HLH, or treatment.
Anemia reflects chronic inflammation, marrow infiltration, hemophagocytosis, bleeding, or hypersplenism.
Thrombocytopenia is a poor prognostic marker and may reflect hypersplenism, marrow involvement, or HLH.
Subcutaneous nodules can represent CAEBV cutaneous infiltration.
Hydroa vacciniforme-like lesions are part of the EBV-positive T/NK LPD spectrum connected to CAEBV.
Severe mosquito bite allergy is a recognized cutaneous CAEBV-related presentation.
EBV-positive mucosal infiltration can produce oral ulcers or aphthous-like lesions.
Gastrointestinal CAEBV can cause ileal, colonic, or duodenal ulceration and mimic IBD or intestinal TB.
CAEBV can involve vessels and produce vasculitic or aneurysmal lesions.
Rare CAEBV cases have EBV-positive lymphoid infiltration associated with orbital myositis.
Rare CAEBV renal involvement can show EBER-positive tubulointerstitial infiltrates and creatinine rise.
CNS involvement, encephalitis-like disease, seizures, shock, or multiorgan failure can produce altered mental status.
CAEBV-associated CNS or vascular disease can produce seizures in selected cases.
Pulmonary lymphoid infiltration, effusions, opportunistic infection, or HLH can cause respiratory failure.
Ferritin rises with macrophage activation and CAEBV-associated HLH.
sCD25 tracks activated T-cell burden in HLH and lymphoma-associated hyperinflammation.
HLH cytokine activity commonly raises triglycerides.
HLH-associated hyperfibrinolysis and consumption lower fibrinogen.
The hidden HLH pressure is expressed clinically as HLH/MAS event risk.
Malignant transformation pressure raises overt EBV-positive lymphoma/leukemia risk.
High tumor turnover and tissue injury can elevate LDH in CAEBV transformation.
HLH is a major cause of rapid CAEBV deterioration and death.
Overt NK/T-cell lymphoma, aggressive NK-cell leukemia, or EBV-positive lymphoma markedly worsens survival.

Total duration of recurrent or persistent CAEBV-like illness. CAEBV typically spans at least 3 months and can persist for years before diagnosis.
Duration of the current fever flare. CAEBV flares often last weeks and recur over months to years.
Recurrent or persistent fever, often 38.5-40 C during active flares.
History of persistent or recurrent fever across weeks to years.
Fatigue, weakness, malaise, and poor stamina from chronic inflammation.
Reduced appetite during inflammatory flares or organ disease.
Inflammatory wasting or lymphoma-like B symptoms during prolonged active disease.
Myalgia can accompany inflammatory CAEBV flares.
Headache may occur with fever or CNS/vascular involvement.
Night sweats can occur as a B-symptom-like inflammatory signal but are not specific for lymphoma.
Cervical, generalized, deep, or PET/CT-detected lymphadenopathy.
Severity or burden of lymphadenopathy when the parent finding is present.
Hepatomegaly from hepatic infiltration or inflammation.
Splenomegaly from reticuloendothelial infiltration and immune activation.
AST can range from mild elevation to marked hepatitis-level values during active hepatic CAEBV or HLH.
ALT can range from mild elevation to marked hepatitis-level values during active hepatic CAEBV or HLH.
Total bilirubin is often normal to mildly elevated but can rise substantially with CAEBV cholestatic hepatitis or liver failure.
Direct bilirubin rises with cholestatic CAEBV hepatitis.
Cholestatic or infiltrative hepatic CAEBV can raise alkaline phosphatase.
GGT rises with cholestatic or infiltrative hepatic involvement.
Albumin can fall with chronic inflammation, liver dysfunction, enteritis, or critical illness.
Often normal or low; lymphocyte expansion, infection, steroid exposure, or HLH phase can change direction.

Can fall with marrow involvement, HLH, chemotherapy, antivirals, or immune deficiency.
Anemia from inflammation, marrow involvement, HLH, bleeding, or hypersplenism.
Platelets may be mildly to severely reduced; thrombocytopenia is a poor prognostic marker and increases bleeding hazard.
LDH rises with lymphoid turnover, tissue infiltration, hepatitis, hemolysis, HLH, or transformation.
CRP is variably elevated; low CRP does not exclude CAEBV because viral/lymphoproliferative inflammation can be discordant.
Ferritin is normal to moderately elevated in chronic inflammation and rises sharply with CAEBV-associated HLH.
Triglycerides increase with HLH physiology and severe systemic inflammation.
Falls with HLH-associated hyperfibrinolysis, consumptive coagulopathy, liver dysfunction, or major bleeding.
Tracks activated T-cell burden, HLH pressure, and lymphoma-associated hyperinflammation.
D-dimer rises with HLH coagulopathy, vascular lesions, bleeding, thrombosis, or critical illness.
Can prolong with coagulopathy, liver dysfunction, or critical illness.
Can rise with liver dysfunction, consumptive coagulopathy, or bleeding complications.
Usually low unless bacterial coinfection, shock, renal dysfunction, or severe inflammatory organ disease coexists.
Peripheral blood EBV DNA load. This is a confirmatory/monitoring axis, not an ordinary presentation observation in case ranking unless explicitly enabled.
EBV VCA IgG positivity supports prior or chronic EBV exposure but is not specific without viral load and tissue evidence.
EBV early antigen IgG activity can support chronic active or reactivated EBV context but is not an ordinary clinical observation.
EBNA IgG indicates past infection; used in virology interpretation rather than ordinary symptom ranking.
EBER-positive lymphocytes in affected tissue or organ biopsy; confirmatory layer evidence.
Probability that EBV is carried by T cells or NK cells based on sorted-cell PCR, flow-FISH, EBER/IHC, or tissue phenotype.
Probability that EBV is carried by B cells based on sorted-cell or tissue studies; changes rituximab relevance.
Tender, recurrent, erythematous, or panniculitis-like subcutaneous nodules due to cutaneous CAEBV infiltration.

Photosensitive papulovesicular or ulcerative hydroa vacciniforme-like eruption within the EBV-positive T/NK LPD spectrum.
Exaggerated mosquito-bite reaction with ulceration, necrosis, fever, lymphadenopathy, or systemic flare.
Non-specific rash or eruption; child axes should describe morphology when available.

Periorbital edema from orbital inflammation, myositis, renal/serosal disease, or systemic inflammation.
Diplopia from orbital myositis or ocular involvement in rare CAEBV cases.
Chronic sinusitis or sinonasal involvement reported in some multisystem cases; not specific and should not substitute for tissue/virology confirmation.
MRI or clinically inferred ocular/orbital myositis due to CAEBV organ infiltration.
Renal tubulointerstitial infiltration by EBV-positive lymphocytes; rare but directly organ-damaging.
Usually normal unless renal infiltration, shock, nephrotoxic therapy, or critical illness occurs.
Endoscopic or pathologic intestinal ulcers from CAEBV gastrointestinal lymphoproliferative disease.
Diarrhea from gastrointestinal CAEBV or treatment complications.
Abdominal pain from hepatitis, splenomegaly, enteritis, vascular lesions, bleeding, or cholecystitis-like complications.
Visible lower gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcerative or vascular CAEBV bowel disease.
Active GI bleeding, occult to massive hemorrhage.
Vasculitic, aneurysmal, or vascular-dilation lesions attributed to EBV-positive lymphoid disease.
Visceral or head/neck arterial aneurysm/vascular lesion burden in CAEBV vascular disease.
Confusion, reduced consciousness, encephalitis-like syndrome, seizures, shock, or critical illness.
Seizures from CNS EBV disease, vascular lesions, metabolic derangement, or critical illness.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP often share cytokine drivers but can be discordant in viral/lymphoproliferative disease.
Both transaminases rise together during CAEBV hepatitis.
Direct bilirubin contributes to total bilirubin in cholestatic hepatitis.
ALP and GGT can rise together during cholestatic/infiltrative hepatic involvement.
Splenic sequestration contributes to thrombocytopenia in CAEBV.
Hypofibrinogenemia during HLH or liver failure increases bleeding risk.
Rising ferritin is a core signal of macrophage activation and HLH risk.
sCD25 reflects activated T-cell burden in HLH and lymphoma-associated hyperinflammation.
Vascular dilation or aneurysmal lesions in CAEBV can cause major GI bleeding.
GI bleeding is a major bleeding pathway in CAEBV GI/vascular disease.
CAEBV-associated HLH can progress quickly to multiorgan failure.
Transformation to aggressive EBV-positive lymphoma or leukemia substantially worsens survival.
Major hemorrhage is a direct fatal pathway in severe CAEBV, especially GI bleeding.
Multiorgan failure is a terminal CAEBV pathway.
Immune dysfunction, chemotherapy, steroids, and HSCT predispose to fatal opportunistic infection.
AKI increases treatment toxicity and multiorgan failure risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Donor availability determines whether curative immune replacement is feasible.
Severe organ dysfunction or uncontrolled infection raises transplant-related mortality.
Organ failure may require disease control before HSCT conditioning.

failure_modes: no suitable donor or delayed donor coordination
treatments.context_specific_role: Curative immune replacement for systemic CAEBV when donor, disease control, and organ-fitness conditions are acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Poor marrow reserve, hepatic dysfunction, or infection limits chemotherapy intensity.
Overt transformation increases the need for lymphoma-directed cytoreduction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Disease control and transformation-directed therapy, often as a bridge to HSCT rather than durable standalone cure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Etoposide/dexamethasone is targeted to severe EBV-HLH physiology rather than indolent CAEBV alone.
Severe hepatic/renal dysfunction requires dose adjustment and changes toxicity.

failure_modes: HLH relapse if CAEBV clone persists
treatments.context_specific_role: Controls CAEBV-associated HLH while definitive CAEBV clone-directed therapy is planned.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids can rapidly reduce HLH-associated cytokine inflammation.
Steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection and obscure diagnosis.

failure_modes: transient fever or LFT response with relapse on taper
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid anti-inflammatory control for severe flare, HLH, organ inflammation, or bridge therapy; not clone-eradicating.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells and is not expected to eradicate T/NK CAEBV.
T/NK-infected CAEBV lacks the CD20 target on the infected clone.

failure_modes: ineffective when EBV is in T/NK cells
treatments.context_specific_role: Useful only when a B-cell EBV reservoir or EBV-positive B-cell LPD component is demonstrated.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: A measurable lytic DNAemia component may fall with antiviral therapy, but latent proliferating lymphocytes often persist.
Ganciclovir and valganciclovir require renal dosing.

failure_modes: does not eradicate latent EBV-infected T/NK clone
treatments.context_specific_role: May reduce lytic EBV DNAemia or organ viral load in selected cases, but is not sufficient clone-eradicating therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Published benefit is concentrated in vascular/intestinal bleeding presentations.
The combination targets hemorrhagic vascular GI involvement rather than systemic clone eradication.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue symptom-control option for rare CAEBV enteritis with vascular lesions and life-threatening GI bleeding.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active bleeding increases the immediate value of transfusion and fibrinogen replacement.

failure_modes: rebleeding if ulcerative or vascular lesion persists

side_effects.interpretation: transfusion-related infection risk is very low but nonzero

treatments.context_specific_role: Stabilizes anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypofibrinogenemia while definitive disease or bleeding-source control is pursued.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Prophylaxis and early treatment matter most during neutropenia, steroids, chemotherapy, or HSCT.

side_effects.interpretation: drug-specific nephrotoxicity or renal dosing context

treatments.context_specific_role: Prevents and treats infection during CAEBV immune dysfunction and treatment-related immunosuppression.

child_or_adolescent.trajectory_modulation: Classical CAEBV often begins in childhood or adolescence and may evolve over years.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Childhood-onset disease can remain indolent for prolonged periods before systemic progression.

adult_onset.trajectory_modulation: Adult systemic CAEBV is less common but may show aggressive organ involvement or transformation.

east_asian_or_latin_american_background.trajectory_modulation: Reported incidence is higher in East Asian and Latin American populations.

other_background.trajectory_modulation: CAEBV still occurs worldwide, including Western cohorts, so absence of this background does not exclude disease.

T_or_NK_cell_CAEBV.trajectory_modulation: Higher probability of systemic inflammatory organ infiltration, HLH, and NK/T transformation.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: T/NK CAEBV is strongly linked to EBV-HLH.
T/NK lineage can evolve into NK/T-cell lymphoma or aggressive NK-cell leukemia.

B_cell_CAEBV.trajectory_modulation: May be more compatible with rituximab-responsive B-cell EBV reservoir in selected cohorts.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: B-cell lineage evidence changes treatment-effect modulation.

high_or_rising_load.trajectory_modulation: High or rising EBV DNA supports active CAEBV burden and is associated with worse prognosis.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: High viral load at diagnosis and persistent burden correlate with severe disease.

multiorgan_extranodal_disease.trajectory_modulation: GI, pulmonary, renal, ocular, CNS, vascular, serosal, or hepatic involvement raises complication and mortality risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: More organ targets increase the chance of irreversible organ failure.

ferritin_scd25_hypofibrinogenemia_or_hem.trajectory_modulation: Does not define CAEBV alone but identifies an aggressive CAEBV complication state.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: HLH is a major poor prognostic feature.

fever_liver_dysfunction_thrombocytopenia.trajectory_modulation: This cluster marks more aggressive CAEBV and worse survival.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Published prognostic factors include liver dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, fever, splenomegaly, anemia, and long time from onset.

primary_or_acquired_cellular_immune_defe.trajectory_modulation: Raises risk for severe EBV disease and may blur boundaries with immunodeficiency-associated EBV LPD; should be explicit context rather than ordinary observation.

chronic_steroids_or_immunosuppressants.trajectory_modulation: Can suppress fever and inflammatory markers while increasing EBV persistence and opportunistic infection risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Immunosuppression and CAEBV treatment both raise infection risk.

donor_available_and_fit_for_hsct.trajectory_modulation: Does not change CAEBV prior probability but strongly changes treatment outcome.

no_donor_or_unfit_for_hsct.trajectory_modulation: Leaves only non-curative or bridge therapies and increases long-term risk.

supportive_care: Keep EBV DNA load, EBER, infected lymphocyte lineage, sorted-cell studies, and biopsy pathology in confirmatory/virology/pathology evidence layers rather than ordinary presentation observations.
Evaluate chronicity explicitly: recurrent or persistent mononucleosis-like illness over at least 3 months is central to CAEBV and separates it from acute EBV infectious mononucleosis.

Exclude near mimics and coexisting diseases with ordinary evidence plus confirmatory context: acute EBV infectious mononucleosis, CMV mono-like illness, HLH/MAS as a complication or mimic, EBV-positive lymphoma, autoimmune flare, disseminated tuberculosis, bacterial sepsis, and drug-induced liver injury.
Repeat CBC with differential, AST/ALT, bilirubin, ALP/GGT, albumin, LDH, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, D-dimer, and sCD25 when fever persists or cytopenias evolve.
Use tissue biopsy when organ involvement is accessible: EBER in situ hybridization plus CD3/CD4/CD8/CD56/CD20/CD30/granzyme/perforin and clonality studies help distinguish CAEBV from overt lymphoma.
Stage organ burden with directed imaging, ultrasound/CT/PET-CT, endoscopy, CNS imaging/CSF testing, renal evaluation, or ophthalmologic workup according to symptoms.
For suspected CAEBV-associated HLH, monitor ferritin, sCD25, fibrinogen, triglycerides, cytopenias, liver injury, coagulation, and hemophagocytosis without treating HLH as the same disease manifold.
Manage bleeding with hemodynamic stabilization, blood products, fibrinogen replacement, endoscopy or embolization when indicated, while addressing the CAEBV intestinal/vascular driver.
Prevent opportunistic infection during steroids, chemotherapy, rituximab, and HSCT; use PJP, antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal strategies according to immunosuppression and neutropenia.

Coordinate hematology, infectious disease, pathology, transplant, hepatology, gastroenterology, ICU, and organ-specific specialists early because diagnosis and treatment depend on tissue lineage, organ burden, and transplant feasibility.
